title: Harry Ross's band and the Connie's Inn gig
summary: Scott joins the Connie's Inn band and learns it has been rented to Dutch Schultz.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: And so, Harry Ross was a member of the Amsterdam. Every year, we used to give a dance at -- up by the Manhatten Casino on 55th Street or the New Star Casino or some big place. And he was considered to be one of the best violinists we had. Harry Ross, did you ever hear of him?
Yeah, only from you, only that I knew you worked with him.

Well, he was going to open up at -- because he was a member of the Amsterdam, and he caught up down at the Amsterdam. I went there one night just to look around. I was still playing the Lafayette. He says, (unintelligible). Connie Simms was right by the Lafayette, but it was downstairs.
Yeah, strictly white, no colored. Leroy Smith had been there 11 years, in Connie's Inn. So you see, he looked like he had a grip on it, and nobody -- and I never

went there and never went in there. Colored people didn't go in there, strictly white people. And I said, where you going, Connie's Inn? He say, yeah. He says, I want you to rehease with us. He named a place and he had a rehearsal band and all like that.

We went in Connie's Inn. Well, there was something different for me, too. Uptown and all, Connie's Inn, strictly white, no colored. It was nice, very nice, very nice. See, they -- Connie, he was the playboy, but George, his brother, he was the businessman. George came to us and said, listen, fellows, says, we're not going to have anybody here tonight. It's sold out to Dutch Schultze. Lord, lord, lord. (Unintelligible) I was scared to death. Dutch Schultz was the biggest gangster in town at that time.

He and his men had rented Connie's Inn. And, lord, to tell the truth, I didn't feel like I could play or nothing. I was scared to death. And I was talking to the fellow next to me, Luke Smith was working with me. Luke Smith, Luke Smith and I were good friends. He was Joe Smith's brother. Luke could play better trumpet than any of the other two. He was the best. But you wouldn't think he did it, because he liked to play pool so much.
Luke was in __________ band, Luke and I were great friends. Luke says, I ain't paying him any mind. I said, why? He says, well, they treat you nice. It'll be all right.
